memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "When Moses enquired about the goat of the sin offering and found that it had been burned up, he was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron's remaining sons, and asked, 'Why didn't you eat the sin offering in the sanctuary area? It is most holy; it was given to you to take away the guilt of the community by making atonement for them before the LORD.'" - Lev 10:16-17 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Moses is angry. After everything that has happened, he discovers another deviation from instruction and confronts Aaron's surviving sons.

It is understandable. Two men have just died for departing from God's commands. Moses is not going to lose two more.

But it is worth noticing what is happening beneath the anger. Moses is afraid. He has just watched fire fall, and now he sees another irregularity. His sharpness comes from care, not cruelty.

We often do this too. Anger that looks like criticism is frequently fear wearing a different face — a parent shouting at a child who ran into the road, a leader coming down hard because they have seen where this road leads.

That does not make harsh words harmless. Paul writes, In your anger do not sin (Eph 4:26) — acknowledging that anger itself is not automatically wrong, while warning where it can go.

If someone has been sharp with you recently, it may be worth asking what they are afraid of. And if you have been sharp with someone, the same question is worth asking of yourself.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Is there anger in me that is really fear or love in disguise?
2. Have I judged someone's sharpness without asking what lay behind it?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, help me to understand what drives my anger and to handle it honestly. Give me grace with those whose sharpness hides fear. Amen.
